{"answer": "# Imitation-Learning Policies on Low-Cost Robot Arms: Benchmarks, Demonstration Requirements, and Comparison with Scripted Motion

## 1. Overview

This report synthesizes the published and preprint literature (2023–2026) on imitation-learning (IL) policies—Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, and π0.5—evaluated on low-cost arms directly relevant to the user's hardware (AgileX PiPER 6-DOF, SO-101 leader/follower). It also positions these results against the established Diffusion Policy benchmark on the UR5 industrial arm. **Caveat:** The majority of SO-101 and AgileX PiPER results are from arXiv preprints (flagged below); only the ALOHA/ACT paper (RSS 2023) and the Diffusion Policy paper (IJRR 2024) have appeared in peer-reviewed venues.

The following table consolidates the main results across platforms, policies, tasks, and evaluation protocols.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## 2. ACT on ALOHA (the Foundational Low-Cost Result)

The most cited low-cost manipulation benchmark is the original ALOHA system by Zhao et al. (RSS 2023, arXiv preprint; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2304.13705). Six real-world bimanual tasks were evaluated with 50 teleoperated demonstrations each (100 for Thread Velcro), one random seed, and 25 evaluation trials per task (pqac-00000015). Object placements were randomized along a 15 cm reference line. Success was defined as sequential subtask completion: for example, Slot Battery required "grasp, place, and fully insert the battery while stabilizing the controller," and Put On Shoe required "fitting and securing the shoe so it remains attached after release" (pqac-00000017). ACT achieved final-subtask success rates of 88% (Slide Ziploc), 96% (Slot Battery), 84% (Open Cup), 20% (Thread Velcro), 64% (Prep Tape), and 92% (Put On Shoe) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000045).

**Protocol you can repeat:** Collect 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task at 50 Hz (8–14 s episodes, 400–700 steps). Randomize object placement within a defined zone. Evaluate the trained policy over 25 trials. Report subtask-level and whole-task binary success rates.

---

## 3. Mobile ALOHA: Co-Training and Open-Loop Replay

Fu et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2024; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2401.02117) extended ALOHA with a mobile base and evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, and VINN on seven mobile-bimanual tasks with 20–50 in-domain demonstrations. Using co-training with existing static ALOHA data, ACT achieved whole-task success rates of 95% (Wipe Wine), 95% (Call Elevator), 85% (Use Cabinet), 85% (High Five), 80% (Rinse Pan), 80% (Push Chairs), and 40% (Cook Shrimp) over 20 trials per task (5 for Cook Shrimp) (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000019). Critically, open-loop replay of demonstrations—even with objects returned to their original positions—yielded 0% whole-task success on every task (pqac-00000046). This is the clearest published demonstration that closed-loop learned policies are categorically superior to open-loop scripted replay on low-cost arms with imprecise base control.

---

## 4. Diffusion Policy on UR5 (Peer-Reviewed Industrial Baseline)

Chi et al. (IJRR, peer-reviewed, 2024; DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273668) benchmarked Diffusion Policy on the real-world Push-T task using a UR5 arm. The policy was trained on 136 demonstrations, evaluated over 20 episodes from matched initial conditions with a 60-second time limit (pqac-00000021). Success was defined as the final intersection-over-union (IoU) exceeding the minimum IoU from the human demonstration dataset. The best end-to-end Transformer Diffusion Policy achieved 95% success with a mean final IoU of 0.80, compared with 100% success and 0.84 IoU for human demonstrations (pqac-00000020). This is the strongest peer-reviewed real-robot Diffusion Policy result and provides a reproducible reference for comparison with low-cost arms.

**Protocol you can repeat:** Use a top-down camera and a T-shaped block. Collect ~136 demonstrations. Evaluate 20 episodes. Compute pixel-space IoU between the block silhouette and a printed target. An episode succeeds if IoU exceeds the minimum human IoU.

---

## 5. SO-101 Benchmarks

### 5.1 Demonstration Scaling on SO-101 (Cowling, 2026)

Cowling (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.37170) conducted a controlled scaling study on a single SO-101 arm, comparing ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and fine-tuned π0.5 on a ball pick-and-place task with two distractor objects. Models were trained on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations and evaluated on ten fixed object placements with a 30-second episode limit, producing 1,340 scored episodes across 126 blocks (pqac-00000001). Key findings:

- **ACT** required between 50 and 100 demonstrations to learn the task. At 12 demonstrations, it reached the ball in only 10% of episodes (6/60). At 100 demonstrations, it achieved 92.5% success (37/40). At 200, performance was 87.5% (35/40) (pqac-00000006).
- **π0.5** (pretrained VLA, fine-tuned) was substantially better with scarce data: 40% (16/40) at 12 demonstrations and ~70% (28/40) at 25, remaining near 70% thereafter. ACT overtook it from 100 demonstrations onward (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000033).
- **Diffusion Policy** peaked near 50% and suffered from an initiation problem—it rarely began moving when demonstrations contained idle lead-in frames, though trimming these frames raised its initiation rate from 4% to 90% (pqac-00000011).
- **SmolVLA** peaked near 50% and failed to start in 47% of episodes (pqac-00000001).

### 5.2 Multi-Task Benchmark on SO-101 (ArmnetBench v0.1)

Selvaraj et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481) evaluated seven policies across 12 tabletop tasks on a fleet of SO-101 cells, with 50 demonstrations per policy per task and generally 30 rollouts per policy-task cell. Operators labeled each rollout as successful, suboptimal, or failed. Aggregate strict success rates were: π0.5 47.6%, π0 35.1%, GR00T N1.7 29.4%, Diffusion Policy 26.7%, ACT 19.2%, MolmoAct 2 18.9%, and SmolVLA 15.0% (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000050). Per-task variation was large; for example, ACT scored 63% on eye_drops_to_basket but 0% on block_stack, while π0.5 scored 86% on transfer_cube and 70% on cable_unclip (pqac-00000050).

### 5.3 Suture Following on SO-101

Wang et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2605.28736) benchmarked ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0 on suture-thread acquisition using a single SO-101 follower arm with a wrist camera and a fixed side camera. 160 teleoperated demonstrations were used, and each policy was evaluated over 20 test episodes (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030). Under the clean-background, dual-camera baseline condition, π0 achieved 75%, Diffusion Policy 65%, SmolVLA 65%, and ACT 50%. π0's advantage was attributed to its pretrained vision-language backbone and data efficiency: it reached 65% success with only 64 demonstrations and remained in the 65–75% range as data increased to 160 (pqac-00000029).

### 5.4 SO-101 Bench: Spatial Manipulation

Hickok (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.36420) defined a language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark (bin, next-to, between, directional-move tasks) with 916 simulation episodes and 3,629 simulated teleoperated demonstrations. On the physical SO-101 with unseen objects, Galaxea 0.5 (a learned policy) achieved 53% (24/45 layouts), while a code-writing LLM agent (GPT-6.1 Sol + PyRUA-Lean) delegating grasps to Galaxea 0.5 reached 64% (29/45) (pqac-00000024). Simulation overestimated success by 9–31 percentage points but preserved the ranking order of five independently trained policies (pqac-00000025).

---

## 6. AgileX PiPER Benchmarks

### 6.1 Action-Space Design Study

Feng et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2602.23408) compared ACT and Diffusion Policy on the AgileX single-arm platform across four action-space representations (absolute/relative end-effector, absolute/relative joint position) on four tasks: Touch Cube, Pick Up Cup, Pick-and-Place Cup, and Bimanual Cube Transfer. Results were averaged over three independent repeats of 10 rollouts. ACT averaged 26.7%–46.3% depending on action space; Diffusion Policy averaged 26.0%–48.0%. The best variant for both was relative joint position (ACT 46.3%, DP 48.0%) (pqac-00000053). Object positions were uniformly initialized across a 6×6 workspace grid to reduce distribution shift (pqac-00000037). The number of training demonstrations was not reported in the retrieved text.

### 6.2 AprilTag + MoveIt2 Pipeline (Simulation Only)

Zhang (thesis, 2026; DOI: 10.32920/32253717) integrated the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm with AprilTag visual detection and MoveIt2 motion planning in NVIDIA Isaac Sim via ROS2. The AprilTag-detected pose was transformed into the world frame for the MoveIt Task Constructor to generate collision-free pick-and-place trajectories (pqac-00000038). However, the thesis reported no quantitative success rates, no comparison with learned policies, and no physical-robot evaluation—only a validated simulation pipeline. **No published peer-reviewed or preprint paper was found that directly compares AprilTag-guided scripted closed-loop manipulation with an imitation-learning policy on the same AgileX PiPER task and evaluation protocol.**

---

## 7. Learned vs. Scripted/Open-Loop: What Has Been Compared?

The following table summarizes the sparse but important evidence on this question.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Three distinct forms of comparison appear in the literature:

1. **Scripted vs. human training data for the same learned policy.** Zhao et al. showed that ACT trained on scripted (programmatic) demonstrations substantially outperformed ACT trained on human demonstrations in simulation. On Cube Transfer, scripted-data ACT achieved 86% on the hardest subtask vs. 50% for human-data ACT (pqac-00000044). This reflects training-data quality, not a learned-vs.-scripted controller contrast.

2. **Open-loop replay vs. closed-loop learned policy.** Fu et al. found that open-loop replay of a demonstration yielded 0% whole-task success on every Mobile ALOHA task, while ACT achieved 40–95% (pqac-00000046). This demonstrates that visual feedback and online correction are essential for low-cost arms with imprecise actuation.

It also positions these results against the established Diffusion Policy benchmark on the UR5 industrial arm. **Caveat:** The majority of SO-101 and AgileX PiPER results are from arXiv preprints (flagged below); only the ALOHA/ACT paper (RSS 2023) and the Diffusion Policy paper (IJRR 2024) have appeared in peer-reviewed venues.

The following table consolidates the main results across platforms, policies, tasks, and evaluation protocols.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## 2. ACT on ALOHA (the Foundational Low-Cost Result)

The most cited low-cost manipulation benchmark is the original ALOHA system by Zhao et al. (RSS 2023, arXiv preprint; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2304.13705). Six real-world bimanual tasks were evaluated with 50 teleoperated demonstrations each (100 for Thread Velcro), one random seed, and 25 evaluation trials per task (pqac-00000015). Object placements were randomized along a 15 cm reference line. Success was defined as sequential subtask completion: for example, Slot Battery required "grasp, place, and fully insert the battery while stabilizing the controller," and Put On Shoe required "fitting and securing the shoe so it remains attached after release" (pqac-00000017). ACT achieved final-subtask success rates of 88% (Slide Ziploc), 96% (Slot Battery), 84% (Open Cup), 20% (Thread Velcro), 64% (Prep Tape), and 92% (Put On Shoe) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000045).

**Protocol you can repeat:** Collect 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task at 50 Hz (8–14 s episodes, 400–700 steps). Randomize object placement within a defined zone. Evaluate the trained policy over 25 trials. Report subtask-level and whole-task binary success rates.

---

## 3. Mobile ALOHA: Co-Training and Open-Loop Replay

Fu et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2024; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2401.02117) extended ALOHA with a mobile base and evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, and VINN on seven mobile-bimanual tasks with 20–50 in-domain demonstrations. Using co-training with existing static ALOHA data, ACT achieved whole-task success rates of 95% (Wipe Wine), 95% (Call Elevator), 85% (Use Cabinet), 85% (High Five), 80% (Rinse Pan), 80% (Push Chairs), and 40% (Cook Shrimp) over 20 trials per task (5 for Cook Shrimp) (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000019). Critically, open-loop replay of demonstrations—even with objects returned to their original positions—yielded 0% whole-task success on every task (pqac-00000046). This is the clearest published demonstration that closed-loop learned policies are categorically superior to open-loop scripted replay on low-cost arms with imprecise base control.

Chi et al. (IJRR, peer-reviewed, 2024; DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273668) benchmarked Diffusion Policy on the real-world Push-T task using a UR5 arm. The policy was trained on 136 demonstrations, evaluated over 20 episodes from matched initial conditions with a 60-second time limit (pqac-00000021). Success was defined as the final intersection-over-union (IoU) exceeding the minimum IoU from the human demonstration dataset. Cowling (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.37170) conducted a controlled scaling study on a single SO-101 arm, comparing ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and fine-tuned π0.5 on a ball pick-and-place task with two distractor objects. - **Scripted vs. human training data:** Scripted-data ACT outperformed human-data ACT by up to 36 percentage points in simulation (pqac-00000044).
- **AprilTag-guided vs. learned:** **No published evidence exists for this comparison on any low-cost arm.**"}

## 1. Overview

This report synthesizes the published and preprint literature (2023–2026) on imitation-learning (IL) policies—Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, and π0.5—evaluated on low-cost arms directly relevant to the user's hardware (AgileX PiPER 6-DOF, SO-101 leader/follower). ---

## 2. ACT on ALOHA (the Foundational Low-Cost Result)

The most cited low-cost manipulation benchmark is the original ALOHA system by Zhao et al. (RSS 2023, arXiv preprint; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2304.13705). Six real-world bimanual tasks were evaluated with 50 teleoperated demonstrations each (100 for Thread Velcro), one random seed, and 25 evaluation trials per task (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8). Object placements were randomized along a 15 cm reference line. Success was defined as sequential subtask completion: for example, Slot Battery required "grasp, place, and fully insert the battery while stabilizing the controller," and Put On Shoe required "fitting and securing the shoe so it remains attached after release" (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 6-7). ACT achieved final-subtask success rates of 88% (Slide Ziploc), 96% (Slot Battery), 84% (Open Cup), 20% (Thread Velcro), 64% (Prep Tape), and 92% (Put On Shoe) (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8, zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 8-10).

**Protocol you can repeat:** Collect 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task at 50 Hz (8–14 s episodes, 400–700 steps). Randomize object placement within a defined zone. Evaluate the trained policy over 25 trials. Report subtask-level and whole-task binary success rates.

---

## 3. Mobile ALOHA: Co-Training and Open-Loop Replay

Fu et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2024; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2401.02117) extended ALOHA with a mobile base and evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, and VINN on seven mobile-bimanual tasks with 20–50 in-domain demonstrations. Using co-training with existing static ALOHA data, ACT achieved whole-task success rates of 95% (Wipe Wine), 95% (Call Elevator), 85% (Use Cabinet), 85% (High Five), 80% (Rinse Pan), 80% (Push Chairs), and 40% (Cook Shrimp) over 20 trials per task (5 for Cook Shrimp) (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8, fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 5-7). Critically, open-loop replay of demonstrations—even with objects returned to their original positions—yielded 0% whole-task success on every task (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8). This is the clearest published demonstration that closed-loop learned policies are categorically superior to open-loop scripted replay on low-cost arms with imprecise base control.

---

## 4. Diffusion Policy on UR5 (Peer-Reviewed Industrial Baseline)

Chi et al. (IJRR, peer-reviewed, 2024; DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273668) benchmarked Diffusion Policy on the real-world Push-T task using a UR5 arm. The policy was trained on 136 demonstrations, evaluated over 20 episodes from matched initial conditions with a 60-second time limit (chi2025diffusionpolicyvisuomotor pages 17-18). Success was defined as the final intersection-over-union (IoU) exceeding the minimum IoU from the human demonstration dataset. The best end-to-end Transformer Diffusion Policy achieved 95% success with a mean final IoU of 0.80, compared with 100% success and 0.84 IoU for human demonstrations (chi2025diffusionpolicyvisuomotor pages 8-9). This is the strongest peer-reviewed real-robot Diffusion Policy result and provides a reproducible reference for comparison with low-cost arms.

**Protocol you can repeat:** Use a top-down camera and a T-shaped block. Collect ~136 demonstrations. Evaluate 20 episodes. Compute pixel-space IoU between the block silhouette and a printed target. An episode succeeds if IoU exceeds the minimum human IoU.

---

## 5. SO-101 Benchmarks

### 5.1 Demonstration Scaling on SO-101 (Cowling, 2026)

Cowling (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.37170) conducted a controlled scaling study on a single SO-101 arm, comparing ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and fine-tuned π0.5 on a ball pick-and-place task with two distractor objects. Models were trained on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations and evaluated on ten fixed object placements with a 30-second episode limit, producing 1,340 scored episodes across 126 blocks (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3). Key findings:

- **ACT** required between 50 and 100 demonstrations to learn the task. At 12 demonstrations, it reached the ball in only 10% of episodes (6/60). At 100 demonstrations, it achieved 92.5% success (37/40). At 200, performance was 87.5% (35/40) (cowling2026from12to pages 19-21).
- **π0.5** (pretrained VLA, fine-tuned) was substantially better with scarce data: 40% (16/40) at 12 demonstrations and ~70% (28/40) at 25, remaining near 70% thereafter. ACT overtook it from 100 demonstrations onward (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3).
- **Diffusion Policy** peaked near 50% and suffered from an initiation problem—it rarely began moving when demonstrations contained idle lead-in frames, though trimming these frames raised its initiation rate from 4% to 90% (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3).
- **SmolVLA** peaked near 50% and failed to start in 47% of episodes (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3).

### 5.2 Multi-Task Benchmark on SO-101 (ArmnetBench v0.1)

Selvaraj et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481) evaluated seven policies across 12 tabletop tasks on a fleet of SO-101 cells, with 50 demonstrations per policy per task and generally 30 rollouts per policy-task cell. Operators labeled each rollout as successful, suboptimal, or failed. Aggregate strict success rates were: π0.5 47.6%, π0 35.1%, GR00T N1.7 29.4%, Diffusion Policy 26.7%, ACT 19.2%, MolmoAct 2 18.9%, and SmolVLA 15.0% (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9). Per-task variation was large; for example, ACT scored 63% on eye_drops_to_basket but 0% on block_stack, while π0.5 scored 86% on transfer_cube and 70% on cable_unclip (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9).

### 5.3 Suture Following on SO-101

Wang et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2605.28736) benchmarked ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0 on suture-thread acquisition using a single SO-101 follower arm with a wrist camera and a fixed side camera. 160 teleoperated demonstrations were used, and each policy was evaluated over 20 test episodes (wang2026imitationlearningfor pages 6-10, wang2026imitationlearningfor pages 10-13). Under the clean-background, dual-camera baseline condition, π0 achieved 75%, Diffusion Policy 65%, SmolVLA 65%, and ACT 50%. π0's advantage was attributed to its pretrained vision-language backbone and data efficiency: it reached 65% success with only 64 demonstrations and remained in the 65–75% range as data increased to 160 (wang2026imitationlearningfor pages 6-10).

### 5.4 SO-101 Bench: Spatial Manipulation

Hickok (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.36420) defined a language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark (bin, next-to, between, directional-move tasks) with 916 simulation episodes and 3,629 simulated teleoperated demonstrations. On the physical SO-101 with unseen objects, Galaxea 0.5 (a learned policy) achieved 53% (24/45 layouts), while a code-writing LLM agent (GPT-6.1 Sol + PyRUA-Lean) delegating grasps to Galaxea 0.5 reached 64% (29/45) (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 2-4). Simulation overestimated success by 9–31 percentage points but preserved the ranking order of five independently trained policies (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 8-10).

---

## 6. AgileX PiPER Benchmarks

### 6.1 Action-Space Design Study

Feng et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2602.23408) compared ACT and Diffusion Policy on the AgileX single-arm platform across four action-space representations (absolute/relative end-effector, absolute/relative joint position) on four tasks: Touch Cube, Pick Up Cup, Pick-and-Place Cup, and Bimanual Cube Transfer. Results were averaged over three independent repeats of 10 rollouts. ACT averaged 26.7%–46.3% depending on action space; Diffusion Policy averaged 26.0%–48.0%. The best variant for both was relative joint position (ACT 46.3%, DP 48.0%) (feng2026demystifyingactionspace pages 21-22). Object positions were uniformly initialized across a 6×6 workspace grid to reduce distribution shift (feng2026demystifyingactionspace pages 4-5). The number of training demonstrations was not reported in the retrieved text.

### 6.2 AprilTag + MoveIt2 Pipeline (Simulation Only)

Zhang (thesis, 2026; DOI: 10.32920/32253717) integrated the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm with AprilTag visual detection and MoveIt2 motion planning in NVIDIA Isaac Sim via ROS2. The AprilTag-detected pose was transformed into the world frame for the MoveIt Task Constructor to generate collision-free pick-and-place trajectories (zhang2026anintegratedsimulation pages 22-27). However, the thesis reported no quantitative success rates, no comparison with learned policies, and no physical-robot evaluation—only a validated simulation pipeline. **No published peer-reviewed or preprint paper was found that directly compares AprilTag-guided scripted closed-loop manipulation with an imitation-learning policy on the same AgileX PiPER task and evaluation protocol.**

---

The following table summarizes the sparse but important evidence on this question.

Three distinct forms of comparison appear in the literature:

1. **Scripted vs. human training data for the same learned policy.** Zhao et al. showed that ACT trained on scripted (programmatic) demonstrations substantially outperformed ACT trained on human demonstrations in simulation. 2. **Open-loop replay vs. closed-loop learned policy.** Fu et al. found that open-loop replay of a demonstration yielded 0% whole-task success on every Mobile ALOHA task, while ACT achieved 40–95% (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8). 3. **No AprilTag-guided closed-loop baseline.** Despite the user's interest in fiducial-guided scripted motion, **no published paper was found that evaluates an AprilTag-guided closed-loop scripted controller alongside an imitation-learning policy on the same low-cost arm, task, and evaluation protocol.** The Zhang 2026 thesis validates an AprilTag + MoveIt2 pipeline for the AgileX PiPER in simulation but reports no learned-policy comparison or quantitative success metrics (zhang2026anintegratedsimulation pages 22-27). This represents a clear gap in the literature and an opportunity for a new contribution.

---

## 8. Cross-Platform Comparison: Low-Cost vs. Industrial Arms

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al., arXiv **preprint**, 2024; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2412.13877) collected 107k demonstrations across Franka, UR5e, AgileX, and humanoid platforms under a unified protocol, evaluating ACT, Diffusion Policy (DP3), and other methods with 10 real-world trials per task (wu2024robomindbenchmarkon pages 9-10). The UR5e achieved generally higher per-task success than the Franka on matching IL methods, with some UR5e tasks reaching 0.5–0.8 while Franka tasks ranged 0.0–0.3 (hou2025robomind2.0a pages 37-39). However, these numbers are task-dependent and the column headers were not fully recoverable from the retrieved text.

**RoboTwin 2.0** (Chen et al., arXiv **preprint**, 2025; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2506.18088) supports five simulated arms—Franka, PiPER, UR5, ARX-X5, and ALOHA-AgileX—with over 100,000 domain-randomized expert trajectories across 50 dual-arm tasks, providing a sim-to-real transfer benchmark relevant to the user's PiPER hardware.

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al., arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2602.22818) provides reference implementations for ACT, Diffusion Policy, VQ-BET, π0, SmolVLA, and HIL-SERL with native support for SO-100, SO-101, and Koch-v1.1 arms. The library integrates the LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks, but the LeRobot paper itself does not report physical-robot task success rates (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 7-10, cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 5-7).

**ABB YuMi and Kinova:** No published paper was found that directly benchmarks ACT or Diffusion Policy on ABB YuMi or Kinova Gen3 arms with comparable evaluation protocols to the low-cost arm studies above. These arms appear in the broader robotics literature for other purposes but have not been subjected to the same IL benchmarks.

---

## 9. Protocols You Can Repeat

Based on the literature, the following evaluation protocols are reproducible on your hardware:

1. **Cowling-style demonstration scaling (SO-101).** Collect 200 teleoperated demonstrations of a single task (e.g., pick-and-place). Train ACT and Diffusion Policy on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations. Evaluate each model on 10 fixed placements × 4 repeats (≈40 trials) with a 30-second episode limit. Score using a four-stage ladder: initiated motion, reached object, grasped/carried, and delivered (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3, cowling2026from12to pages 19-21).

2. **ArmnetBench-style multi-task (SO-101).** Select a subset of the 12 ArmnetBench tasks (e.g., block stacking, ring insertion, cable clipping). Collect 50 demonstrations per task. Evaluate each policy with 30 rollouts per task-policy pair. Label rollouts as successful, suboptimal, or failed (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7).

3. **Push-T style (AgileX PiPER or SO-101).** Print a T-block target template. Collect ~136 demonstrations. Evaluate 20 episodes from matched initial conditions with a 60-second limit. Compute IoU from a top-down camera (chi2025diffusionpolicyvisuomotor pages 17-18).

4. **AgileX PiPER curriculum (four tasks).** Use the Feng et al. four-task progression (Touch Cube → Pick Up Cup → Pick-and-Place Cup → Bimanual Cube Transfer). Divide the workspace into a 6×6 grid, uniformly initialize objects, and evaluate 3 trials × 10 rollouts per action-space variant (feng2026demystifyingactionspace pages 4-5, feng2026demystifyingactionspace pages 21-22).

---

## 10. Key Gaps and Opportunities

- **No peer-reviewed head-to-head comparison of AprilTag-guided scripted closed-loop motion vs. imitation learning on the same low-cost arm exists.** This is the most directly actionable gap for your setup.
- **No published IL benchmark results for ABB YuMi or Kinova Gen3** using ACT or Diffusion Policy were found.
- **Most SO-101 and PiPER results are from 2026 arXiv preprints** with zero or few citations. None have undergone formal peer review at the time of this search.
- **Trial counts on low-cost arms are generally small** (10–40 per condition), limiting statistical power. Cowling explicitly warns that "ten episodes per model is generally insufficient" (cowling2026from12to pages 21-24).
- **Demonstration counts for the AgileX PiPER action-space study (Feng et al.) were not reported** in the retrieved text, limiting reproducibility (feng2026demystifyingactionspace pages 21-22).

---

## 11. Summary of Key Quantitative Findings

- **ACT on ALOHA:** 50 demonstrations, 25 trials, 84–96% on moderate tasks, 20% on the hardest (Thread Velcro) (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8).
- **ACT on SO-101:** Needs ~50–100 demonstrations to become effective; 92.5% at 100 demonstrations on a pick-and-place task (cowling2026from12to pages 19-21).
- **Diffusion Policy on UR5 (peer-reviewed):** 136 demonstrations, 20 trials, 95% success on Push-T (chi2025diffusionpolicyvisuomotor pages 8-9).
- **Diffusion Policy on SO-101:** Peaked near 50% on pick-and-place (Cowling) and 26.7% aggregate across 12 diverse tasks (ArmnetBench) (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9).
- **π0/π0.5 (pretrained VLAs) on SO-101:** Best with scarce data (40% at 12 demos for π0.5); 47.6% aggregate across 12 tasks (ArmnetBench) (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9).
- **ACT and DP on AgileX PiPER:** 26–48% success depending on action-space representation; relative joint-position commands performed best (feng2026demystifyingactionspace pages 21-22).
- **Open-loop replay vs. learned:** 0% vs. 40–95% on Mobile ALOHA (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8).
- **Scripted vs. human training data:** Scripted-data ACT outperformed human-data ACT by up to 36 percentage points in simulation (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8).
- **AprilTag-guided vs. learned:** **No published evidence exists for this comparison on any low-cost arm.**

---

## 2. ACT on ALOHA (the Foundational Low-Cost Result)

The most cited low-cost manipulation benchmark is the original ALOHA system by Zhao et al. (RSS 2023, arXiv preprint; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2304.13705). Six real-world bimanual tasks were evaluated with 50 teleoperated demonstrations each (100 for Thread Velcro), one random seed, and 25 evaluation trials per task (pqac-00000015). Object placements were randomized along a 15 cm reference line. Success was defined as sequential subtask completion: for example, Slot Battery required "grasp, place, and fully insert the battery while stabilizing the controller," and Put On Shoe required "fitting and securing the shoe so it remains attached after release" (pqac-00000017). ACT achieved final-subtask success rates of 88% (Slide Ziploc), 96% (Slot Battery), 84% (Open Cup), 20% (Thread Velcro), 64% (Prep Tape), and 92% (Put On Shoe) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000045).

**Protocol you can repeat:** Collect 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task at 50 Hz (8–14 s episodes, 400–700 steps). Randomize object placement within a defined zone. Evaluate the trained policy over 25 trials. Report subtask-level and whole-task binary success rates.

---

## 3. Mobile ALOHA: Co-Training and Open-Loop Replay

Fu et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2024; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2401.02117) extended ALOHA with a mobile base and evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, and VINN on seven mobile-bimanual tasks with 20–50 in-domain demonstrations. Using co-training with existing static ALOHA data, ACT achieved whole-task success rates of 95% (Wipe Wine), 95% (Call Elevator), 85% (Use Cabinet), 85% (High Five), 80% (Rinse Pan), 80% (Push Chairs), and 40% (Cook Shrimp) over 20 trials per task (5 for Cook Shrimp) (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000019). Critically, open-loop replay of demonstrations—even with objects returned to their original positions—yielded 0% whole-task success on every task (pqac-00000046). This is the clearest published demonstration that closed-loop learned policies are categorically superior to open-loop scripted replay on low-cost arms with imprecise base control.

---

## 4. Diffusion Policy on UR5 (Peer-Reviewed Industrial Baseline)

Chi et al. (IJRR, peer-reviewed, 2024; DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273668) benchmarked Diffusion Policy on the real-world Push-T task using a UR5 arm. The policy was trained on 136 demonstrations, evaluated over 20 episodes from matched initial conditions with a 60-second time limit (pqac-00000021). Success was defined as the final intersection-over-union (IoU) exceeding the minimum IoU from the human demonstration dataset. The best end-to-end Transformer Diffusion Policy achieved 95% success with a mean final IoU of 0.80, compared with 100% success and 0.84 IoU for human demonstrations (pqac-00000020). This is the strongest peer-reviewed real-robot Diffusion Policy result and provides a reproducible reference for comparison with low-cost arms.

**Protocol you can repeat:** Use a top-down camera and a T-shaped block. Collect ~136 demonstrations. Evaluate 20 episodes. Compute pixel-space IoU between the block silhouette and a printed target. An episode succeeds if IoU exceeds the minimum human IoU.

---

## 5. SO-101 Benchmarks

### 5.1 Demonstration Scaling on SO-101 (Cowling, 2026)

Cowling (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.37170) conducted a controlled scaling study on a single SO-101 arm, comparing ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and fine-tuned π0.5 on a ball pick-and-place task with two distractor objects. Models were trained on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations and evaluated on ten fixed object placements with a 30-second episode limit, producing 1,340 scored episodes across 126 blocks (pqac-00000001). Key findings:

- **ACT** required between 50 and 100 demonstrations to learn the task. At 12 demonstrations, it reached the ball in only 10% of episodes (6/60). At 100 demonstrations, it achieved 92.5% success (37/40). At 200, performance was 87.5% (35/40) (pqac-00000006).
- **π0.5** (pretrained VLA, fine-tuned) was substantially better with scarce data: 40% (16/40) at 12 demonstrations and ~70% (28/40) at 25, remaining near 70% thereafter. ACT overtook it from 100 demonstrations onward (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000033).
- **Diffusion Policy** peaked near 50% and suffered from an initiation problem—it rarely began moving when demonstrations contained idle lead-in frames, though trimming these frames raised its initiation rate from 4% to 90% (pqac-00000011).
- **SmolVLA** peaked near 50% and failed to start in 47% of episodes (pqac-00000001).

### 5.2 Multi-Task Benchmark on SO-101 (ArmnetBench v0.1)

Selvaraj et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481) evaluated seven policies across 12 tabletop tasks on a fleet of SO-101 cells, with 50 demonstrations per policy per task and generally 30 rollouts per policy-task cell. Operators labeled each rollout as successful, suboptimal, or failed. Aggregate strict success rates were: π0.5 47.6%, π0 35.1%, GR00T N1.7 29.4%, Diffusion Policy 26.7%, ACT 19.2%, MolmoAct 2 18.9%, and SmolVLA 15.0% (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000050). Per-task variation was large; for example, ACT scored 63% on eye_drops_to_basket but 0% on block_stack, while π0.5 scored 86% on transfer_cube and 70% on cable_unclip (pqac-00000050).

### 5.3 Suture Following on SO-101

Wang et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2605.28736) benchmarked ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0 on suture-thread acquisition using a single SO-101 follower arm with a wrist camera and a fixed side camera. 160 teleoperated demonstrations were used, and each policy was evaluated over 20 test episodes (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030). Under the clean-background, dual-camera baseline condition, π0 achieved 75%, Diffusion Policy 65%, SmolVLA 65%, and ACT 50%. π0's advantage was attributed to its pretrained vision-language backbone and data efficiency: it reached 65% success with only 64 demonstrations and remained in the 65–75% range as data increased to 160 (pqac-00000029).

### 5.4 SO-101 Bench: Spatial Manipulation

Hickok (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.36420) defined a language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark (bin, next-to, between, directional-move tasks) with 916 simulation episodes and 3,629 simulated teleoperated demonstrations. On the physical SO-101 with unseen objects, Galaxea 0.5 (a learned policy) achieved 53% (24/45 layouts), while a code-writing LLM agent (GPT-6.1 Sol + PyRUA-Lean) delegating grasps to Galaxea 0.5 reached 64% (29/45) (pqac-00000024). Simulation overestimated success by 9–31 percentage points but preserved the ranking order of five independently trained policies (pqac-00000025).

---

## 6. AgileX PiPER Benchmarks

### 6.1 Action-Space Design Study

Feng et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2602.23408) compared ACT and Diffusion Policy on the AgileX single-arm platform across four action-space representations (absolute/relative end-effector, absolute/relative joint position) on four tasks: Touch Cube, Pick Up Cup, Pick-and-Place Cup, and Bimanual Cube Transfer. Results were averaged over three independent repeats of 10 rollouts. ACT averaged 26.7%–46.3% depending on action space; Diffusion Policy averaged 26.0%–48.0%. The best variant for both was relative joint position (ACT 46.3%, DP 48.0%) (pqac-00000053). Object positions were uniformly initialized across a 6×6 workspace grid to reduce distribution shift (pqac-00000037). The number of training demonstrations was not reported in the retrieved text.

### 6.2 AprilTag + MoveIt2 Pipeline (Simulation Only)

Zhang (thesis, 2026; DOI: 10.32920/32253717) integrated the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm with AprilTag visual detection and MoveIt2 motion planning in NVIDIA Isaac Sim via ROS2. The AprilTag-detected pose was transformed into the world frame for the MoveIt Task Constructor to generate collision-free pick-and-place trajectories (pqac-00000038). However, the thesis reported no quantitative success rates, no comparison with learned policies, and no physical-robot evaluation—only a validated simulation pipeline. **No published peer-reviewed or preprint paper was found that directly compares AprilTag-guided scripted closed-loop manipulation with an imitation-learning policy on the same AgileX PiPER task and evaluation protocol.**

---

## 7. Learned vs. Scripted/Open-Loop: What Has Been Compared?

The following table summarizes the sparse but important evidence on this question.

*Table: Comparison of the limited matched evidence for learned policies, scripted training data, and open-loop replay, plus demonstration-scaling results on SO-101. It also identifies the unresolved absence of an AprilTag-guided versus imitation-learning comparison on the same low-cost physical task.*

Three distinct forms of comparison appear in the literature:

1. **Scripted vs. human training data for the same learned policy.** Zhao et al. showed that ACT trained on scripted (programmatic) demonstrations substantially outperformed ACT trained on human demonstrations in simulation. On Cube Transfer, scripted-data ACT achieved 86% on the hardest subtask vs. 50% for human-data ACT (pqac-00000044). This reflects training-data quality, not a learned-vs.-scripted controller contrast.

2. **Open-loop replay vs. closed-loop learned policy.** Fu et al. found that open-loop replay of a demonstration yielded 0% whole-task success on every Mobile ALOHA task, while ACT achieved 40–95% (pqac-00000046). This demonstrates that visual feedback and online correction are essential for low-cost arms with imprecise actuation.

3. **No AprilTag-guided closed-loop baseline.** Despite the user's interest in fiducial-guided scripted motion, **no published paper was found that evaluates an AprilTag-guided closed-loop scripted controller alongside an imitation-learning policy on the same low-cost arm, task, and evaluation protocol.** The Zhang 2026 thesis validates an AprilTag + MoveIt2 pipeline for the AgileX PiPER in simulation but reports no learned-policy comparison or quantitative success metrics (pqac-00000038). This represents a clear gap in the literature and an opportunity for a new contribution.

---

## 8. Cross-Platform Comparison: Low-Cost vs. Industrial Arms

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al., arXiv **preprint**, 2024; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2412.13877) collected 107k demonstrations across Franka, UR5e, AgileX, and humanoid platforms under a unified protocol, evaluating ACT, Diffusion Policy (DP3), and other methods with 10 real-world trials per task (pqac-00000049). The UR5e achieved generally higher per-task success than the Franka on matching IL methods, with some UR5e tasks reaching 0.5–0.8 while Franka tasks ranged 0.0–0.3 (pqac-00000047). However, these numbers are task-dependent and the column headers were not fully recoverable from the retrieved text.

**RoboTwin 2.0** (Chen et al., arXiv **preprint**, 2025; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2506.18088) supports five simulated arms—Franka, PiPER, UR5, ARX-X5, and ALOHA-AgileX—with over 100,000 domain-randomized expert trajectories across 50 dual-arm tasks, providing a sim-to-real transfer benchmark relevant to the user's PiPER hardware.

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al., arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2602.22818) provides reference implementations for ACT, Diffusion Policy, VQ-BET, π0, SmolVLA, and HIL-SERL with native support for SO-100, SO-101, and Koch-v1.1 arms. The library integrates the LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks, but the LeRobot paper itself does not report physical-robot task success rates (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000042).

**ABB YuMi and Kinova:** No published paper was found that directly benchmarks ACT or Diffusion Policy on ABB YuMi or Kinova Gen3 arms with comparable evaluation protocols to the low-cost arm studies above. These arms appear in the broader robotics literature for other purposes but have not been subjected to the same IL benchmarks.

---

## 9. Protocols You Can Repeat

Based on the literature, the following evaluation protocols are reproducible on your hardware:

1. **Cowling-style demonstration scaling (SO-101).** Collect 200 teleoperated demonstrations of a single task (e.g., pick-and-place). Train ACT and Diffusion Policy on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations. Evaluate each model on 10 fixed placements × 4 repeats (≈40 trials) with a 30-second episode limit. Score using a four-stage ladder: initiated motion, reached object, grasped/carried, and delivered (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006).

2. **ArmnetBench-style multi-task (SO-101).** Select a subset of the 12 ArmnetBench tasks (e.g., block stacking, ring insertion, cable clipping). Collect 50 demonstrations per task. Evaluate each policy with 30 rollouts per task-policy pair. Label rollouts as successful, suboptimal, or failed (pqac-00000052).

3. **Push-T style (AgileX PiPER or SO-101).** Print a T-block target template. Collect ~136 demonstrations. Evaluate 20 episodes from matched initial conditions with a 60-second limit. Compute IoU from a top-down camera (pqac-00000021).

4. **AgileX PiPER curriculum (four tasks).** Use the Feng et al. four-task progression (Touch Cube → Pick Up Cup → Pick-and-Place Cup → Bimanual Cube Transfer). Divide the workspace into a 6×6 grid, uniformly initialize objects, and evaluate 3 trials × 10 rollouts per action-space variant (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000053).

---

## 10. Key Gaps and Opportunities

- **No peer-reviewed head-to-head comparison of AprilTag-guided scripted closed-loop motion vs. imitation learning on the same low-cost arm exists.** This is the most directly actionable gap for your setup.
- **No published IL benchmark results for ABB YuMi or Kinova Gen3** using ACT or Diffusion Policy were found.
- **Most SO-101 and PiPER results are from 2026 arXiv preprints** with zero or few citations. None have undergone formal peer review at the time of this search.
- **Trial counts on low-cost arms are generally small** (10–40 per condition), limiting statistical power. Cowling explicitly warns that "ten episodes per model is generally insufficient" (pqac-00000002).
- **Demonstration counts for the AgileX PiPER action-space study (Feng et al.) were not reported** in the retrieved text, limiting reproducibility (pqac-00000053).

---

## 11. Summary of Key Quantitative Findings

- **ACT on ALOHA:** 50 demonstrations, 25 trials, 84–96% on moderate tasks, 20% on the hardest (Thread Velcro) (pqac-00000015).
- **ACT on SO-101:** Needs ~50–100 demonstrations to become effective; 92.5% at 100 demonstrations on a pick-and-place task (pqac-00000006).
- **Diffusion Policy on UR5 (peer-reviewed):** 136 demonstrations, 20 trials, 95% success on Push-T (pqac-00000020).
- **Diffusion Policy on SO-101:** Peaked near 50% on pick-and-place (Cowling) and 26.7% aggregate across 12 diverse tasks (ArmnetBench) (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000050).
- **π0/π0.5 (pretrained VLAs) on SO-101:** Best with scarce data (40% at 12 demos for π0.5); 47.6% aggregate across 12 tasks (ArmnetBench) (pqac-00000039).
- **ACT and DP on AgileX PiPER:** 26–48% success depending on action-space representation; relative joint-position commands performed best (pqac-00000053).
- **Open-loop replay vs. learned:** 0% vs. 40–95% on Mobile ALOHA (pqac-00000046).
- **Scripted vs. human training data:** Scripted-data ACT outperformed human-data ACT by up to 36 percentage points in simulation (pqac-00000044).
- **AprilTag-guided vs. learned:** **No published evidence exists for this comparison on any low-cost arm.**

contexts.context: The excerpt reports a low-cost robot-arm benchmark involving reaching a ball, grasping it, and carrying/manipulating it. Evaluation used staged episodes and typically 40 trials per condition; the ACT comparison at 12 demonstrations used 60 trials. ACT required between 50 and 100 demonstrations to learn the task under its default recipe. At 12 demonstrations, ACT reached the ball in 6/60 episodes (10%), whereas fine-tuned π0.5 reached it in 27/40 (67.5%). Fine-tuned π0.5 was substantially better than policies trained from scratch below 50 demonstrations, but the excerpt does not provide a complete success-rate table for every policy and demonstration count. For ACT, success was 37/40 at 100 demonstrations (92.5%) and 35/40 at 200 (87.5%); first-grasp accuracy was slightly worse at 200, although chunk-to-chunk agreement improved. SmolVLA’s success rose through 50 demonstrations and then held through 200, while its first-grasp accuracy continued rising; its main limitation was episode initiation. Diffusion Policy’s initiation rate improved from 4% to 90% after trimming idle lead-in frames, but overall success figures are not given in this excerpt. The passage also notes that success was judged alongside reaching, first-grasp accuracy, manipulation, carrying, and initiation, with about 40 trials per cell and roughly 25 percentage-point resolution.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports ULOHA experiments using low-cost leader–follower underwater arms and three imitation-learning policies: ACT, Diffusion Policy, and SmolVLA. However, the supplied section provides quantitative task results only for ACT; it states that Diffusion Policy and SmolVLA were deployed, but does not give their success rates or demonstration counts here. ACT used one separately trained policy per task, a 100-step execution horizon, and ten evaluation trials per task. The first seven tasks used ten demonstrations each, while the final two buoyancy-driven sponge tasks used 50 demonstrations each. Success required reaching the task-specific state within the episode limit and retaining it at episode end. ACT success rates were: block hand-over 10/10 (100%), hand-over then place 6/10 (60%), block stacking 9/10 (90%), sequential transfer 10/10 (100%), bimanual lifting 10/10 (100%), cooperative insertion 9/10 (90%), lid opening 7/10 (70%), surface hand-over 4/10 (40%), and release and catch 3/10 (30%). The benchmark criteria included successful transfer without floor contact, stable stacking, joint lifting, insertion, lid removal, floating-sponge transfer, and catching a rising sponge before it reached the surface.

Demonstration counts were ten per task for the first seven tasks and 50 demonstrations for the final two buoyancy-driven sponge tasks (surface hand-over and release and catch). Success required reaching the task-specific target state within the step limit and retaining that state at episode end. Reported ACT results were respectively 10/10, 6/10, 9/10, 10/10, 10/10, 9/10, 7/10, 4/10, and 3/10. The task-specific criteria included transferring without floor contact, placing fully inside a target, stable stacking, completing successive route legs, jointly lifting clear of the floor, inserting a block into an upright cup, removing a lid while holding its container, transferring a floating sponge, and catching a released sponge before it reached the surface. contexts.context: The excerpt reports ACT/ALOHA benchmarks on two simulated tasks and six real-world tasks. contexts.context: SO-101 Bench evaluates language-conditioned spatial manipulation in simulation using four task types: placing an object in a bin, placing one object next to another, placing an object between two references, and moving an object directionally. These are organized into five task families and tested across 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance, and unseen-class splits. The benchmark contains 916 evaluation episodes, covering 15 task/split cells, with additional ROBUST, PLAN, and MEM subsets for held-out visual appearances, rotate-to-fit planning, and occlusion memory. Policies are fine-tuned using 3,629 simulated teleoperated demonstrations. The reported leaderboard evaluates nine VLAs and world-action models: GPT-6.1 Sol with Galaxea 0.5 (83.2%), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with Galaxea 0.5 (66.8%), InternW0-Δ with Galaxea 0.5 (60.8%), GR00T N1.7 (45.8%), π0.5 (41.0%), LaWAM (39.9%), MolmoAct2 base (23.8%), MolmoAct2-SO101 (20.9%), and FLUX 3 Action (8.0%). The strongest learned policies reach about 61%, while the code-writing LLM agent achieves 83.2%. Five simulation-trained policies preserve their exact ranking on the physical SO-101 arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects, although simulation overestimates success; individual real-robot rates are not specified in this excerpt.
contexts.question: What benchmark tasks and results does SO-101 Bench report? What policies are evaluated, how many demonstrations, how many trials, and what success rates are achieved on the SO-101 arm?

contexts.context: SO-101 Bench evaluates language-conditioned spatial manipulation with one SO-101 arm across four automatically scored tasks: putting every object in a bin, placing one object next to another, placing it between two objects, and moving it directionally until reaching a boundary object. It uses seen-object, unseen-object/seen-class, and unseen-class splits, plus ROBUST, PLAN, and MEM subsets. The primary benchmark contains 916 feasibility-checked episodes across 15 task-family-by-split cells. All learned policies are fine-tuned using the same 3,629 simulated teleoperated demonstrations and equal compute budget; the released datasets also include approximately 4,400 real episodes. The reported leaderboard covers nine VLAs/WAMs and two LLM agents. InternW0-∆ and Galaxea 0.5 are statistically tied near 61 overall, while no learned policy exceeds 17% on PLAN. GPT-6.1 Sol, using the PyRUA-Lean code harness and Galaxea 0.5 for grasping, scores 83.2 overall in simulation and solves 75% of PLAN. In 60 paired episodes, Sol achieves 35% with direct tool calls, 67% with PyRUA-Lean, and 85% with the Galaxea hand-off. On the physical SO-101, the hand-off system reaches 64% (29/45), compared with 53% (24/45) for Galaxea 0.5 alone. Simulation exactly matches the real-robot policy ranking, although it overestimates success by 9–31 percentage points.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports the controlled SO-101 suture-following benchmark using 160 demonstrations for each policy. Under the clean baseline condition with dual cameras, ACT achieved 50% success, Diffusion Policy 65%, SmolVLA 65%, and π0 75%. The corresponding failure distributions were: ACT—25% lateral and 25% depth errors; Diffusion Policy—0% lateral and 35% depth errors; SmolVLA—10% lateral and 25% depth errors; and π0—5% lateral and 20% depth errors. The benchmark used a strict episode-level protocol: success required the gripper to make millimeter-precise contact with the suture thread on a stationary tissue phantom, and surgeon intervention was not permitted. The excerpt also states that camera-view ablations removed either the side or on-arm camera, substantially reducing performance, confirming that the dual-camera setup was necessary. The reported trial count is not explicitly tied to the success-rate table in this excerpt, although the task-completion-time table used 20 trials per policy. In a separate in-loop trial, π0 completed 23 of 25 individual stitches (92%), but that protocol allowed minor surgeon adjustments and therefore is not directly equivalent to the controlled benchmark.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the benchmark as a comparison of ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0 for suture following on an open-source robot arm, with 160 teleoperated demonstrations totaling 32,374 frames. The policies were evaluated across 32 configurations that varied dataset size, camera viewpoint, and background variation. Under ideal conditions, the four policies collectively achieved approximately 50–75% task success, and depth error was reported as the dominant failure mode across architectures. π0 performed best overall, particularly when using a pretrained vision–language backbone; the excerpt characterizes it as more data-efficient, more robust to background variation, and capable of smoother trajectories. In a separate surgeon–robot suturing trial, π0 achieved a 92% stitch completion rate. contexts.context: The benchmark compared ACT, Diffusion Policy, π0, and SmolVLA on the suture-following task using 160 expert demonstration episodes as the full training set. Dataset-size experiments used 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% of the demonstrations, corresponding to 32, 64, 96, 128, and 160 episodes. Under the reported baseline condition—dual cameras, 100% of the training data, and a clean background—ACT achieved 50% success, Diffusion Policy 65%, SmolVLA 65%, and π0 75%. Thus, π0 was the strongest model, while SmolVLA matched Diffusion Policy despite being smaller. The data-efficiency result highlighted π0’s advantage: it reached 65% success with only 64 demonstrations and remained in a 65–75% range thereafter; the other policies generally improved as more demonstrations were added. Each policy was evaluated over 20 test episodes. In every episode, a human held the trailing suture taut and stationary in a randomized direction, the tissue phantom was placed at a randomized workspace position, and the robot acted autonomously. Success required visually locating, approaching, and acquiring the suture thread with the gripper, without intervention. The excerpt does not explicitly identify the robot as SO-101, although it describes the benchmark setup and results.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes evaluation protocols and task definitions for AgileX dual-arm manipulation experiments, but it does not identify the robot as the PiPER arm, name the evaluated policies, or report task-by-task benchmark success rates. The tested tasks were unscrew bottle cap, tic-tac-toe, block into bowl, hot-dog serving, toss blocks into bowl, pour blocks, and clothes folding. Success required complete task completion. Tic-tac-toe involved playing against a human, with the robot alternating whether it moved first and success defined as winning or drawing. Block placement required putting a specified white, red, or green block in a bowl; hot-dog serving required distributing two buns and two sausages so each of two plates received one of each; tossing required putting all six scattered blocks into a bowl; pouring required emptying blocks from a cup into a blue container and returning both arms home; and clothes folding used an operator completion score. The three reference tasks—unscrew bottle cap, tic-tac-toe, and block into bowl—used three trials at 1× speed. The remaining four used ten trials, while time and token measurements came from the first three trials. Pour-blocks trials used 0.8 speed. Timing included execution, model, network, motion, retries, recovery, verification, and human waiting.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the real-world benchmark protocol for the AgileX Piper dual-arm robot (alongside the Zerith H1). Three tabletop manipulation tasks were tested: mouse placement, charger packing, and trash disposal. For each platform, policies were post-trained separately for every task using 200 demonstrations per task; the 600 demonstrations were then combined for five epochs of multitask post-training. Each method was evaluated under two policy-pretraining regimes: with and without large-scale robot-data pretraining. Evaluation used 10 trials per task and setting, producing 60 trials per platform and 120 across both platforms. The settings were in-distribution (ID/EASY), using familiar objects and initial configurations, and out-of-distribution (OOD/HARD), involving unseen mouse poses, unfamiliar chargers and cables, and larger trash collections with unseen objects. The excerpt specifies task success and scoring: mouse placement succeeds when the mouse ends on the pad; charger packing requires both the charger body and entire cable to be inside the receptacle, with partial completion scored 0.25 for the body and 0.75 for the cable; trash disposal requires transferring every designated object into the bin. However, the supplied pages do not include the numerical benchmark success rates or identify the specific policy names.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports ArmnetBench v0.1 using LeRobot v3.0, which stores synchronized state and action data, packed AV1 video, sparse terminal reward and done fields, and episode metadata such as success and policy identity. The benchmark contains 12 tasks across single-arm and bimanual embodiments, including block stacking, cable manipulation, inserting tools or rings, handling eye drops, folding a towel, inserting a candle, opening a lamp door, and transferring a cube. Each policy received the same 50-demonstration training budget. Evaluation used strict success rate over scored rollouts, alongside a more lenient success-plus-suboptimal metric. contexts.context: The comparison evaluates learned policies on two simulated bimanual tasks—Cube Transfer and Bimanual Insertion—using either scripted demonstrations or human demonstrations. Success rates are reported as scripted | human for each subtask. ACT performs best under both data sources. On Cube Transfer, ACT achieves 97|82% for Touch, 90|60% for Lift, and 86|50% for Transfer. On Bimanual Insertion, it achieves 93|76% for Grasp, 90|66% for Contact, and 32|20% for Insert. The other policies are substantially weaker, particularly when trained on human data: BC-ConvMLP reaches 34|3, 17|1, and 1|0% on Cube Transfer, while BeT reaches 60|16, 51|13, and 27|1%; on Bimanual Insertion, their corresponding rates are 5|0, 1|0, 1|0% and 21|0, 4|0, 3|0%. RT-1 and VINN are also generally low. For the six real-world ALOHA tasks, demonstrations are collected through teleoperation and results use human demonstrations only; there is no scripted-versus-human split reported. ACT substantially outperforms the baselines on these tasks as well, including 92% or higher on most subtasks, whereas BeT often has zero success on later subtasks.

It does provide limited information about human-operated evaluation and ACT’s failures. The user study involved six computer-science graduate students, with randomized task order, controller frequency, and initial object position; each operator received two minutes of adaptation followed by three recorded attempts. For ACT, the excerpt reports two difficult tasks where learning failed: candy unwrapping and opening a flat ziploc bag. In an initial 10-trial candy evaluation, the policy picked up the candy in 10/10 trials, pulled both ends in 8/10, but successfully unwrapped it in 0/10. Under a more extensive protocol of 10 trials for each of five candies, it successfully unwrapped three of five candies. For the ziploc task, a policy trained on 50 demonstrations could consistently pick up the bag but struggled with three subsequent mid-air manipulation steps. These figures concern learned-policy performance only and cannot establish scripted-versus-human demonstration success rates.

Other reported whole-task rates with co-training are 95% for Wipe Wine, 40% for Cook Shrimp, 85% for Use Cabinet, 80% for Push Chairs, and 85% for High Five. contexts.context: The excerpt does not report a separate scripted-policy baseline with task-by-task success rates, nor does it provide a direct numerical comparison between scripted data and human demonstration data. It does state that open-loop replay of a demonstration—even with objects restored to their original configurations—achieves 0% whole-task success on all the described mobile-manipulation tasks. The authors attribute this failure to errors from mobile-base velocity control and emphasize that successful execution requires a learned closed-loop policy to react and correct online. In contrast, learned policies perform substantially better: with co-training from static ALOHA data, ACT achieves 95% on Wipe Wine, 95% on Call Elevator, 85% on Use Cabinet, 85% on High Five, 80% on Rinse Pan, and 80% on Push Chairs; Cook Shrimp is reported at 40%. The excerpt also says that VINN with chunking, Diffusion Policy, and ACT all perform well on Mobile ALOHA and benefit from co-training. Thus, the available comparison is 0% for open-loop scripted/demonstration replay versus high task success for learned closed-loop policies, but exact success rates for “scripted data” versus human demonstrations are not included here.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not include the specific per-task success-rate table for ACT, Diffusion Policy, pi0, pi0.5, SmolVLA, or the other evaluated policies, so those numerical rates cannot be recovered from pages 1–3. It does establish the evaluation design: ArmnetBench v0.1 compared seven policies across 12 manipulation tasks on low-cost SO-101 cells, using both single-arm and bimanual configurations. Every policy was trained or fine-tuned with the same budget of 50 demonstrations per task. The benchmark recorded 2,518 policy rollouts and 600 reference demonstrations; the broader released labelled corpus contains 3,718 episodes, including 3,118 core benchmark episodes and 600 additional rollouts. Policy rollouts were evaluated by human operators using three labels—successful, suboptimal, or failure—rather than only binary success. The arm farm ran policy rollouts in isolated containers under a shared protocol, with a fixed nominal cell setup within each task and randomized object positions between rollouts. The leaderboard was intended as an initial comparison under the shared demonstration budget, not as an estimate of each policy’s maximum capability. Later sections or tables of the paper would be needed to identify the individual per-task success rates and the complete policy list.

It does establish the benchmark design and evaluation protocol. ArmnetBench v0.1 contains 12 tabletop tasks, including eight single-arm tasks, and each task-policy combination was trained or fine-tuned using exactly 50 human-teleoperated reference demonstrations. Seven policies were evaluated: ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, π0.5, GR00T N1.7, and MolmoAct 2. Each task-policy pair targeted 30 rollouts, with one π0 and one π0.5 episode removed because of incorrect manual resets, leaving those pairs with 29 valid episodes. Before each rollout, an operator reset the scene and randomized object placement within a task-specific range; initial states were independently sampled across policies. Operators assigned one of three labels—successful, suboptimal, or failure—through the control panel. v0.1 did not impose standardized wall-clock limits, so termination depended on operator judgment.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We have a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and compare them with industrial and research arms (e.g. UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) using tests we can repeat ourselves.

Learned vs scripted: How well have imitation-learning policies (ACT, diffusion policy, LeRobot policies) performed on low-cost arms, and how many demonstrations did they need? How do they compare with scripted or fiducial-guided motion on the same task?

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


# Imitation-Learning Policies on Low-Cost Robot Arms: Benchmarks, Demonstration Requirements, and Comparison with Scripted Motion

## 1. Overview

This report synthesizes the published and preprint literature (2023–2026) on imitation-learning (IL) policies—Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, π0, and π0.5—evaluated on low-cost arms directly relevant to the user's hardware (AgileX PiPER 6-DOF, SO-101 leader/follower). It also positions these results against the established Diffusion Policy benchmark on the UR5 industrial arm. **Caveat:** The majority of SO-101 and AgileX PiPER results are from arXiv preprints (flagged below); only the ALOHA/ACT paper (RSS 2023) and the Diffusion Policy paper (IJRR 2024) have appeared in peer-reviewed venues.

## 2. ACT on ALOHA (the Foundational Low-Cost Result)

The most cited low-cost manipulation benchmark is the original ALOHA system by Zhao et al. (RSS 2023, arXiv preprint; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2304.13705). Six real-world bimanual tasks were evaluated with 50 teleoperated demonstrations each (100 for Thread Velcro), one random seed, and 25 evaluation trials per task (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8). Object placements were randomized along a 15 cm reference line. Success was defined as sequential subtask completion: for example, Slot Battery required "grasp, place, and fully insert the battery while stabilizing the controller," and Put On Shoe required "fitting and securing the shoe so it remains attached after release" (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 6-7). ACT achieved final-subtask success rates of 88% (Slide Ziploc), 96% (Slot Battery), 84% (Open Cup), 20% (Thread Velcro), 64% (Prep Tape), and 92% (Put On Shoe) (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8, zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 8-10).

**Protocol you can repeat:** Collect 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task at 50 Hz (8–14 s episodes, 400–700 steps). Randomize object placement within a defined zone. Evaluate the trained policy over 25 trials. Report subtask-level and whole-task binary success rates.

## 3. Mobile ALOHA: Co-Training and Open-Loop Replay

Fu et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2024; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2401.02117) extended ALOHA with a mobile base and evaluated ACT, Diffusion Policy, and VINN on seven mobile-bimanual tasks with 20–50 in-domain demonstrations. Using co-training with existing static ALOHA data, ACT achieved whole-task success rates of 95% (Wipe Wine), 95% (Call Elevator), 85% (Use Cabinet), 85% (High Five), 80% (Rinse Pan), 80% (Push Chairs), and 40% (Cook Shrimp) over 20 trials per task (5 for Cook Shrimp) (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8, fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 5-7). Critically, open-loop replay of demonstrations—even with objects returned to their original positions—yielded 0% whole-task success on every task (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8). This is the clearest published demonstration that closed-loop learned policies are categorically superior to open-loop scripted replay on low-cost arms with imprecise base control.

## 4. Diffusion Policy on UR5 (Peer-Reviewed Industrial Baseline)

Chi et al. (IJRR, peer-reviewed, 2024; DOI: 10.1177/02783649241273668) benchmarked Diffusion Policy on the real-world Push-T task using a UR5 arm. The policy was trained on 136 demonstrations, evaluated over 20 episodes from matched initial conditions with a 60-second time limit (chi2025diffusionpolicyvisuomotor pages 17-18). Success was defined as the final intersection-over-union (IoU) exceeding the minimum IoU from the human demonstration dataset. The best end-to-end Transformer Diffusion Policy achieved 95% success with a mean final IoU of 0.80, compared with 100% success and 0.84 IoU for human demonstrations (chi2025diffusionpolicyvisuomotor pages 8-9). This is the strongest peer-reviewed real-robot Diffusion Policy result and provides a reproducible reference for comparison with low-cost arms.

**Protocol you can repeat:** Use a top-down camera and a T-shaped block. Collect ~136 demonstrations. Evaluate 20 episodes. Compute pixel-space IoU between the block silhouette and a printed target. An episode succeeds if IoU exceeds the minimum human IoU.

## 5. SO-101 Benchmarks

### 5.1 Demonstration Scaling on SO-101 (Cowling, 2026)

Cowling (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.37170) conducted a controlled scaling study on a single SO-101 arm, comparing ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and fine-tuned π0.5 on a ball pick-and-place task with two distractor objects. Models were trained on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 demonstrations and evaluated on ten fixed object placements with a 30-second episode limit, producing 1,340 scored episodes across 126 blocks (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3). Key findings:

- **ACT** required between 50 and 100 demonstrations to learn the task. At 12 demonstrations, it reached the ball in only 10% of episodes (6/60). At 100 demonstrations, it achieved 92.5% success (37/40). At 200, performance was 87.5% (35/40) (cowling2026from12to pages 19-21).
- **π0.5** (pretrained VLA, fine-tuned) was substantially better with scarce data: 40% (16/40) at 12 demonstrations and ~70% (28/40) at 25, remaining near 70% thereafter. ACT overtook it from 100 demonstrations onward (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3).
- **Diffusion Policy** peaked near 50% and suffered from an initiation problem—it rarely began moving when demonstrations contained idle lead-in frames, though trimming these frames raised its initiation rate from 4% to 90% (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3).
- **SmolVLA** peaked near 50% and failed to start in 47% of episodes (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3).

### 5.2 Multi-Task Benchmark on SO-101 (ArmnetBench v0.1)

Selvaraj et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2607.24481) evaluated seven policies across 12 tabletop tasks on a fleet of SO-101 cells, with 50 demonstrations per policy per task and generally 30 rollouts per policy-task cell. Operators labeled each rollout as successful, suboptimal, or failed. Aggregate strict success rates were: π0.5 47.6%, π0 35.1%, GR00T N1.7 29.4%, Diffusion Policy 26.7%, ACT 19.2%, MolmoAct 2 18.9%, and SmolVLA 15.0% (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9). Per-task variation was large; for example, ACT scored 63% on eye_drops_to_basket but 0% on block_stack, while π0.5 scored 86% on transfer_cube and 70% on cable_unclip (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 7-9).

### 5.3 Suture Following on SO-101

Wang et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2605.28736) benchmarked ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0 on suture-thread acquisition using a single SO-101 follower arm with a wrist camera and a fixed side camera. 160 teleoperated demonstrations were used, and each policy was evaluated over 20 test episodes (wang2026imitationlearningfor pages 6-10, wang2026imitationlearningfor pages 10-13). Under the clean-background, dual-camera baseline condition, π0 achieved 75%, Diffusion Policy 65%, SmolVLA 65%, and ACT 50%. π0's advantage was attributed to its pretrained vision-language backbone and data efficiency: it reached 65% success with only 64 demonstrations and remained in the 65–75% range as data increased to 160 (wang2026imitationlearningfor pages 6-10).

### 5.4 SO-101 Bench: Spatial Manipulation

Hickok (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.36420) defined a language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark (bin, next-to, between, directional-move tasks) with 916 simulation episodes and 3,629 simulated teleoperated demonstrations. On the physical SO-101 with unseen objects, Galaxea 0.5 (a learned policy) achieved 53% (24/45 layouts), while a code-writing LLM agent (GPT-6.1 Sol + PyRUA-Lean) delegating grasps to Galaxea 0.5 reached 64% (29/45) (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 2-4). Simulation overestimated success by 9–31 percentage points but preserved the ranking order of five independently trained policies (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 8-10).

## 6. AgileX PiPER Benchmarks

### 6.1 Action-Space Design Study

Feng et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2602.23408) compared ACT and Diffusion Policy on the AgileX single-arm platform across four action-space representations (absolute/relative end-effector, absolute/relative joint position) on four tasks: Touch Cube, Pick Up Cup, Pick-and-Place Cup, and Bimanual Cube Transfer. Results were averaged over three independent repeats of 10 rollouts. ACT averaged 26.7%–46.3% depending on action space; Diffusion Policy averaged 26.0%–48.0%. The best variant for both was relative joint position (ACT 46.3%, DP 48.0%) (feng2026demystifyingactionspace pages 21-22). Object positions were uniformly initialized across a 6×6 workspace grid to reduce distribution shift (feng2026demystifyingactionspace pages 4-5). The number of training demonstrations was not reported in the retrieved text.

### 6.2 AprilTag + MoveIt2 Pipeline (Simulation Only)

Zhang (thesis, 2026; DOI: 10.32920/32253717) integrated the AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm with AprilTag visual detection and MoveIt2 motion planning in NVIDIA Isaac Sim via ROS2. The AprilTag-detected pose was transformed into the world frame for the MoveIt Task Constructor to generate collision-free pick-and-place trajectories (zhang2026anintegratedsimulation pages 22-27). However, the thesis reported no quantitative success rates, no comparison with learned policies, and no physical-robot evaluation—only a validated simulation pipeline. **No published peer-reviewed or preprint paper was found that directly compares AprilTag-guided scripted closed-loop manipulation with an imitation-learning policy on the same AgileX PiPER task and evaluation protocol.**

It also identifies the unresolved absence of an AprilTag-guided versus imitation-learning comparison on the same low-cost physical task.*

Three distinct forms of comparison appear in the literature:

1. **Scripted vs. human training data for the same learned policy.** Zhao et al. showed that ACT trained on scripted (programmatic) demonstrations substantially outperformed ACT trained on human demonstrations in simulation. On Cube Transfer, scripted-data ACT achieved 86% on the hardest subtask vs. 50% for human-data ACT (zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanual pages 7-8). This reflects training-data quality, not a learned-vs.-scripted controller contrast.

2. **Open-loop replay vs. closed-loop learned policy.** Fu et al. found that open-loop replay of a demonstration yielded 0% whole-task success on every Mobile ALOHA task, while ACT achieved 40–95% (fu2401mobilealohalearning pages 7-8). This demonstrates that visual feedback and online correction are essential for low-cost arms with imprecise actuation.

3. **No AprilTag-guided closed-loop baseline.** Despite the user's interest in fiducial-guided scripted motion, **no published paper was found that evaluates an AprilTag-guided closed-loop scripted controller alongside an imitation-learning policy on the same low-cost arm, task, and evaluation protocol.** The Zhang 2026 thesis validates an AprilTag + MoveIt2 pipeline for the AgileX PiPER in simulation but reports no learned-policy comparison or quantitative success metrics (zhang2026anintegratedsimulation pages 22-27). This represents a clear gap in the literature and an opportunity for a new contribution.

## 8. Cross-Platform Comparison: Low-Cost vs. Industrial Arms

**RoboMIND** (Wu et al., arXiv **preprint**, 2024; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2412.13877) collected 107k demonstrations across Franka, UR5e, AgileX, and humanoid platforms under a unified protocol, evaluating ACT, Diffusion Policy (DP3), and other methods with 10 real-world trials per task (wu2024robomindbenchmarkon pages 9-10). The UR5e achieved generally higher per-task success than the Franka on matching IL methods, with some UR5e tasks reaching 0.5–0.8 while Franka tasks ranged 0.0–0.3 (hou2025robomind2.0a pages 37-39). However, these numbers are task-dependent and the column headers were not fully recoverable from the retrieved text.

**RoboTwin 2.0** (Chen et al., arXiv **preprint**, 2025; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2506.18088) supports five simulated arms—Franka, PiPER, UR5, ARX-X5, and ALOHA-AgileX—with over 100,000 domain-randomized expert trajectories across 50 dual-arm tasks, providing a sim-to-real transfer benchmark relevant to the user's PiPER hardware.

**LeRobot** (Cadène et al., arXiv **preprint**, 2026; DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2602.22818) provides reference implementations for ACT, Diffusion Policy, VQ-BET, π0, SmolVLA, and HIL-SERL with native support for SO-100, SO-101, and Koch-v1.1 arms. The library integrates the LIBERO and Meta-World simulation benchmarks, but the LeRobot paper itself does not report physical-robot task success rates (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 7-10, cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 5-7).

**ABB YuMi and Kinova:** No published paper was found that directly benchmarks ACT or Diffusion Policy on ABB YuMi or Kinova Gen3 arms with comparable evaluation protocols to the low-cost arm studies above. These arms appear in the broader robotics literature for other purposes but have not been subjected to the same IL benchmarks.
